body:
Why environmental footprints are measured

Different activities place different kinds of pressure on the environment. An activity may emit greenhouse gases, consume freshwater, require extraction of minerals or place demands on productive ecosystems.

An environmental footprint is a measure of a specified environmental pressure associated with a product, person, organisation, sector or population. Different footprints measure different aspects of resource use and environmental impact. They should not be combined or compared as though they had the same unit.

Four important footprint concepts

FootprintWhat it measuresTypical unit
Carbon footprintGreenhouse gas emissions associated with an activity or productkg or tonnes of CO2-equivalent
Water footprintSpecified forms of freshwater appropriation and pollution across production or consumptionVolume of water
Material footprintRaw materials extracted globally to satisfy a population's or economy's final demandTonnes of materials
Ecological FootprintDemand placed on biologically productive land and water areasGlobal hectares

Carbon footprint

A carbon footprint accounts for greenhouse gas emissions, usually expressed as carbon dioxide-equivalent (CO2e). The common unit allows gases with different warming effects to be represented in a comparable measure.

A product's carbon footprint may include emissions from raw material production, manufacturing, transport, use and disposal, depending on the assessment boundary. Carbon footprint is not a direct measure of material consumption, water use or biodiversity loss.

The 3 components of a water footprint

The Water Footprint Network distinguishes 3 components:

  • Green water footprint: Rainwater stored in soil and consumed through plant growth, mainly through evaporation and transpiration.
  • Blue water footprint: Surface water or groundwater consumed, such as water evaporated or incorporated into a product rather than returned to the relevant water system.
  • Grey water footprint: The theoretical volume of freshwater needed to assimilate a pollutant load to meet specified water-quality standards.

Green water is associated with rainfall stored in the soil, while blue water is associated with rivers, lakes and aquifers. Grey water footprint is a pollution-related indicator; it does not simply mean the physical quantity of grey-coloured wastewater discharged.

Material footprint

The material footprint of an economy estimates the raw material extraction occurring worldwide to satisfy its final demand. It accounts for materials embodied in imported products, including upstream extraction that may occur outside the importing country.

For example, importing a finished electronic device can involve raw material extraction abroad that is much greater than the physical mass of the device. A material footprint seeks to account for these wider material requirements.

Ecological Footprint

The Ecological Footprint estimates human demand on biologically productive land and water areas needed to provide resources and support the absorption of certain wastes, including the carbon component within that accounting framework.

It is expressed in global hectares, a unit that adjusts biologically productive area to world-average productivity. It can be compared with biocapacity, which represents the regenerative capacity of ecosystems.

When a population's Ecological Footprint exceeds the biocapacity available to it under the chosen accounting boundary, it has an ecological deficit in that accounting comparison.

Domestic Material Consumption versus material footprint

Domestic Material Consumption (DMC) measures materials directly used within an economy. Its basic accounting relationship is:

DMC = Domestic material extraction + Physical material imports − Physical material exports.

DMC uses the direct mass of traded goods. It does not fully attribute the upstream raw materials extracted abroad to produce imported finished goods.

Material footprint instead assigns the worldwide raw-material requirements of products and services to the final demand they satisfy. For this reason, a country's DMC and material footprint can differ substantially.

Under SDG 12, Indicator 12.2.1 concerns material footprint, while Indicator 12.2.2 concerns domestic material consumption. Both indicators have total, per-capita and GDP-related measures.

Intensity and total impact

Footprint per unit of output is an intensity measure. Total footprint is an aggregate measure. A falling carbon footprint per product does not guarantee falling total emissions if the number of products rises sufficiently.

Prelims focus

  • Carbon footprint is generally expressed in CO2-equivalent.
  • Water footprints are classified as green, blue and grey.
  • Grey water footprint represents a calculated pollution-assimilation requirement.
  • Ecological Footprint and biocapacity are expressed in global hectares.
  • SDG Indicator 12.2.1 is material footprint; Indicator 12.2.2 is domestic material consumption.
  • Trap: DMC and material footprint are not interchangeable because their treatment of international supply chains differs.

[Sources: Water Footprint Network, The Water Footprint Assessment Manual, sections defining green, blue and grey water footprints; Global Footprint Network, 'Ecological Footprint', 'What Biocapacity Measures' and 'Glossary', consulted 1 November 2026; United Nations Statistics Division, The Sustainable Development Goals Report 2018, Goal 12, section 'Extraction of raw materials in the developing world is supporting the consumption patterns of richer nations'; United Nations Statistics Division, The Sustainable Development Goals Report 2025, Goal 12, section on domestic material consumption; United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, 'Goal 12', Indicators 12.2.1 and 12.2.2, consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Green, blue and grey water footprints describe different kinds of water use and pressure.

title: Environmental Footprints: Carbon, Water, Material and Ecological Footprints

body:
What is sustainable consumption and production?

Sustainable Consumption and Production (SCP) aims to meet people's needs and improve quality of life while reducing unnecessary resource use, pollution and waste throughout the life cycle of goods and services.

It concerns both sides of the economy. Producers influence material selection, manufacturing methods, packaging and product durability. Consumers influence purchasing decisions, frequency of use, maintenance, food waste and disposal.

Sustainable consumption is not simply purchasing products marketed as environmentally friendly. Avoiding unnecessary purchases, extending the life of existing goods and using resources responsibly are also important.

Environmental labels and certification

Consumers often cannot directly observe how much electricity an appliance uses or how a product affects the environment. Labels can communicate selected performance information and help buyers compare products.

However, different labels measure different characteristics. An energy-efficiency label does not necessarily assess the complete environmental performance of a product.

India's BEE Standards and Labelling Programme

The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), under the Ministry of Power, administers India's Standards and Labelling Programme. The programme was launched in 2006.

For applicable products, the programme uses an energy-performance rating from 1 to 5 stars, with 5 stars indicating greater energy efficiency within the relevant product category and rating conditions.

The rating system helps compare energy performance, but actual electricity consumption also depends on appliance size, operating hours and user behaviour. Star-rating thresholds can change with product category and rating period, so comparisons must use applicable and comparable labels.

India's Ecomark framework

Ecomark is an environmental labelling framework intended to help identify products meeting specified environmental criteria. It considers environmental attributes beyond a single measure of electricity consumption.

The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change notified the Ecomark Rules on 26 September 2024, replacing the earlier Ecomark scheme of 1991. According to the ministry's announcement of 4 October 2024, implementation involves the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) in partnership with the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS).

FeatureBEE star labelEcomark
Principal purposeCommunicate energy efficiencyCommunicate compliance with specified environmental criteria
Main institutionsBEECPCB in partnership with BIS
Key fact1–5 star energy rating; launched in 20062024 Rules replaced the 1991 scheme

An environmental label must also be distinguished from an unsupported advertising claim. General statements such as 'green' or 'eco-friendly', without a clearly defined basis, may mislead consumers. A credible label should have identifiable criteria and appropriate verification.

Green public procurement

Green public procurement means that government buyers consider relevant environmental performance when purchasing goods, services or works. Public purchasing can encourage the market for durable, efficient and less-polluting products.

For instance, a public office buying air conditioners can consider relevant energy-efficiency requirements as well as price and suitability. When replacing lighting equipment, it can consider electricity use, expected life and maintenance requirements.

Life-cycle costing considers costs incurred beyond the initial purchase. These can include energy or water costs, maintenance, repair and disposal. The Department of Expenditure's Manual for Procurement of Goods, Second Edition, 2024 explains total cost of ownership and life-cycle cost as part of assessing value for money.

Procurement must still satisfy applicable government rules, technical needs and fair purchasing procedures. A product is not automatically the best choice merely because its initial price is lowest or its advertisement makes a broad environmental claim.

Behavioural change and Mission LiFE

Improved technology works best when supported by responsible behaviour. An efficient appliance still wastes electricity if left operating unnecessarily. A reusable bag saves resources only when it is actually used repeatedly under suitable conditions.

India's Mission LiFE stands for Lifestyle for Environment. The LiFE concept was introduced at the 2021 COP26 climate conference.

According to a Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change announcement dated 5 June 2023, Mission LiFE had identified 75 individual actions across 7 themes:

  • Save water.
  • Save energy.
  • Reduce waste.
  • Reduce electronic waste.
  • Reduce single-use plastics.
  • Adopt sustainable food systems.
  • Adopt healthy lifestyles.

Useful daily practices include preventing food waste, repairing faulty goods where practical, choosing appropriate reusable products, segregating waste and using electricity and water carefully.

The SDG connection

SDG Target 12.3 seeks to halve per-capita global food waste at retail and consumer levels by 2030 and reduce food losses along production and supply chains. Target 12.7 addresses sustainable public procurement. Target 12.8 concerns public information and awareness for sustainable development and lifestyles by 2030.

Prelims focus

  • BEE's Standards and Labelling Programme was launched in 2006.
  • For applicable appliance categories, BEE uses a 1–5 star energy-efficiency rating.
  • The Ecomark Rules were notified on 26 September 2024, replacing the 1991 scheme.
  • Ecomark implementation involves CPCB and BIS.
  • Mission LiFE means Lifestyle for Environment; a 2023 ministry release identified 75 actions across 7 themes.
  • Trap: A BEE energy-efficiency rating is not a complete life-cycle environmental certification.

[Sources: Bureau of Energy Efficiency, 'Check Testing', Standards and Labelling Programme overview, consulted 1 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, 'Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change notifies Ecomark Rules under Lifestyle for Environment initiative', 4 October 2024, Release ID 2061878; Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance, Manual for Procurement of Goods, Second Edition, 2024, sections 1.6–1.7; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, 'World Environment Day 2023 celebrated with a thrust on Mission LiFE', 5 June 2023, Release ID 1929939; United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, 'Goal 12', Targets 12.3, 12.7 and 12.8, consulted 1 November 2026.]
